children: The Japanese equipment maker will initially import core systems from Japan, while its ATS partnership targets India’s emerging fab and OSAT market and evaluates the scale needed for domestic production

Japanese semiconductor equipment maker Hirata Corporation expects its India business to reach USD 70–100 million by 2030 as semiconductor fabrication and advanced packaging projects move towards commercial operations.
The company, however, said it will consider manufacturing equipment locally only when customer demand is large and recurring enough to justify dedicated production capacity.

Hirata is entering India through an exclusive distribution partnership with ATS India, extending a relationship with its parent company SK International that has existed for more than a decade across sectors including automotive. The initial model will involve supplying core equipment from Japan while ATS India handles local sales, engineering, integration, service and support, company executives told BW Businessworld on the sidelines of Semicon India 2026.

"We think by 2030 this will be a hundred-million-dollar business. So, based on the fabs that are coming and the automation that is required, I think this equipment side of the business would easily hit between USD 70 to 100 million," Kishen Kavikondala, CEO at ATS India said.

He added that the project opportunity is linked to the automation equipment required by semiconductor fabs and other facilities being developed in India. The opportunity covers Hirata's equipment business as well as its ability to support global semiconductor customers operating in the country.

"India represents one of the most important growth markets for Hirata as global semiconductor and electronics manufacturing continues to diversify," said John Derzy, Vice President at Hirata Corporation of America. The company's localisation plans, however, will depend on whether Indian customers generate enough recurring demand to justify domestic production.

The company's initial product portfolio includes Equipment Front End Modules (EFEMs), FOPLP load ports, panel-level packaging handling robots and wafer handling robots. While standard products will continue to be manufactured at Hirata's established facilities, the company is evaluating local engineering, system integration and, eventually, manufacturing as the customer base expands.

Kavikondala said the companies had held discussions with government officials about the support required for industrialisation and automation, identifying workforce training and an enabling policy environment as priorities.
Local Manufacturing Depends On Demand

On manufacturing ambition, Derzy said the company does not have a fixed timetable for manufacturing in India. Instead, the decision will depend on whether the domestic market generates enough annual demand to support production.

"I think that it's part of our long-term strategy. Let's put it that way. So the timing of it is entirely dependent upon how fast the customer base ramps up here and demands enough product that it has to be built locally," Derzy said

Hirata's initial India model will involve importing standard products from Japan, robots and load ports among them — with system-level engineering and integration handled closer to customers. Derzy said the threshold could involve several hundred robots a year, hundreds of load ports and a few hundred EFMs, reflecting the investment and operating requirements associated with local production.

"In terms of robots, there would have to be several hundred robots per year. In terms of EFMs and load ports, sort of the same way. Load ports, you're looking at hundreds of units per year. those are much more involved, much more intense in terms of how you build them and so forth. So you're looking at a few hundred of those as well."

Derzy added that with spare capacity still available in Japan, there's no immediate pressure to localise. He added that if Hirata does eventually manufacture in India, the output would stay domestic rather than feed export markets — again pointing to China as the precedent: "If we manufacture in India, we want to be able to manufacture in India for India. And not the rest of the world. Similar to what we're doing in China. We're manufacturing in China for only China."
OSAT Opens Another Market

Hirata is also targeting India's outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) segment, where automation is required for handling semiconductor packages, trays, strips and other production media. Derzy said OSAT could offer opportunities for customised automation because the requirements can differ from standard equipment applications.
Hirata's existing configurations can be adapted for individual production lines, allowing the company to combine standard components with customer-specific engineering.

"OSAT business right now is something that we want to reach into and work with. Many of our competitors do not do OSAT type of business. That is much more custom than it is just catalogue product. And so we have a lot of core building blocks, baselines type of configurations that we can customise to achieve solutions," Derzy said.

He revealed that Hirata has approached several potential customers in India but declined to name them, adding that the company prioritises customers with continuing equipment needs over one-off sales.
